content: The relationship between vegetable consumption and ferritin concentration (less than 20 μg/L) was not observed when examining higher frequencies of vegetable intake or the likelihood of having very low iron stores (less than 15 μg/L). Similarly, Silva (2007) found no association between the consumption of fruits and vegetables (FV) and non-plant sources (NPS) with the prevalence of anemia. These findings may be influenced by the fact that vegetables and NPS primarily provide non-heme iron, which is less bioavailable unless consumed with vitamin C, despite their iron content. The authors concluded that the purpose of this review was to identify the optimal frequency, variety, and quantity of FV and/or NPS consumption for achieving beneficial dietary and health outcomes. The findings were intended to guide the development of updated WHO Infant and Young Child Feeding (IYCF) guidelines, as well as inform future policies and programs related to complementary feeding. However, the review revealed a lack of high-quality and relevant data to support immediate implications for practice and policy. Instead, it highlighted a significant gap in the evidence, necessitating further research. The review emphasized the need for more studies investigating the effects of different frequencies, varieties, and amounts of FV and NPS consumption during the complementary feeding period and their associations with dietary and health outcomes. Future research should include controlled before-and-after studies or longitudinal cohort studies with internal comparator groups to accurately assess outcomes across groups. Additionally, it is critical to address potential confounding factors in study analyses. Given the global scale of the nutrition transition, future research should also explore the secondary objective of determining the health and nutritional effects of processed/commercial versus fresh/home-prepared foods in the context of optimal complementary feeding practices, including FV and NPS consumption.
